questions.q: How much more light does Webb gather than Hubble?
questions.do: Click the Webb button and read Light gathered, compared with Hubble's 4.0 m² under What it can make out.
questions.a: 25.4 m², about 6.4 times Hubble's 4.0 m². A bigger mirror collects more light, so it can see fainter objects.

questions.q: Could Hubble see the Apollo lunar module left on the Moon?
questions.do: Click Hubble and leave the Colour of light observed slider at its starting value (about 501 nm). Read the Smallest detail for The Moon in the table.
questions.a: No. Hubble's smallest detail on the Moon is about 98 m, but the lunar module is only 4 m wide. It is far smaller than one blur disc.

questions.q: For Hubble, how does the sharpest detail change when you switch from violet light to red light?
questions.do: Click Hubble. Move the Colour of light observed slider to about 400 nm (violet) and read Sharpest detail at this colour. Then move it to about 700 nm (red) and read it again.
questions.a: About 42 milliarcseconds in violet and about 73 milliarcseconds in red. The blur disc is 1.22 λ/D, so a longer wavelength gives a bigger disc and a less sharp image.

questions.q: Why must Webb be kept colder than 50 K?
questions.do: In Why Webb has to be so cold, set Temperature of the glowing object to 300 K and read where the glow peaks. Then set it to 50 K.
questions.a: At 300 K the glow peaks at about 9.7 µm, inside Webb's 0.6–28.5 µm range, so a warm Webb would be dazzled by itself. At 50 K the peak moves to about 58 µm, out of the way. Peak wavelength = 2,898 ÷ temperature (Wien's law).

questions.q: Hubble (1990), India's AstroSat (2015) and Webb (2021) were launched years apart. Which has the biggest mirror, and can AstroSat UVIT split the two stars that Hubble splits?
questions.do: Click each of Hubble, AstroSat UVIT and Webb and read the Mirror line. Keep both sliders at their starting values and read the message under the star picture for Hubble and for AstroSat UVIT.
questions.a: Mirrors: Hubble 2.4 m, AstroSat UVIT 38 cm, Webb 6.5 m, the biggest. Hubble shows Two stars (1.2 disc-widths apart). AstroSat UVIT shows One blob (0.19 disc-widths), because its smaller mirror makes a bigger blur disc.
